value.distinction: Layer is an architectural scope; protocol implements peer communication.
A PDU becomes an SDU when passed to the lower layer.
Sender adds metadata downward; receiver strips it upward.
Service describes functionality; protocol defines peer behavior.
Physical sends signals; link frames and controls directly connected nodes.
Link is node-to-node; network crosses different networks.
Network routes packets; transport manages application data sequences.
Session manages dialogs; transport manages end-to-end transfer.
Presentation translates data; application provides high-level services.
OSI explicitly has seven layers; TCP/IP uses broader functional scopes.
Some functions, especially security and management, span layers.
Conceptual architecture differs from the protocols originally designed for it.
Bit is logical information; signal is physical representation.
Transport may maintain connection state or not.

value.misconception: Every protocol fits cleanly in one layer.

value.misconception: Every PDU is called a packet.

value.misconception: Each layer is a separate physical device.
value.correction: Layers are abstractions that may be implemented across software and hardware.

Network delivery need not be reliable.
The source includes multiple transport protocols and connection modes.

value.misconception: TCP/IP has a mandatory session layer.
value.correction: TCP/IP does not distinguish a separate session layer.
It also covers translation, encoding, and compression.

value.misconception: OSI and TCP/IP layers are identical.
value.correction: The source gives approximate mappings and important differences.

value.misconception: OSI protocols became the dominant Internet stack.
value.correction: TCP/IP became widespread while OSI protocols did not gain broad popularity.

source_claims.claim: OSI is a seven-layer reference model.
Each layer serves the layer above and is served by the layer below.
Layer peers exchange PDUs through layer protocols.
Encapsulation adds headers/footers while moving downward.
Decapsulation strips headers/footers while moving upward.
Physical layer defines signal/media properties.
Data link provides node-to-node transfer and link control.
Network layer provides multi-network delivery and routing.
Transport provides end-to-end/application transfer and QoS functions.
Security and management are cross-layer functions.
OSI does not define implementation-specific programming APIs.
TCP/IP mapping to OSI is approximate.
OSI was standardized through ISO/CCITT work and published in 1984.

source_claims.title: Identity and design
source_claims.statement: Python is high-level, general-purpose, multi-paradigm, readability-oriented, indentation-based, standard-library-rich and garbage-collected.

source_claims.title: Origin
source_claims.statement: Python was conceived by Guido van Rossum at CWI as a successor to ABC; implementation began in 1989 and first release was 0.9.0 in 1991.

source_claims.title: Governance
source_claims.statement: Guido left the BDFL role in 2018 and a five-member Steering Council was elected in 2019.

source_claims.title: Version history
source_claims.statement: Python 2.0 added major features; Python 3.0 was a major non-fully-compatible revision; typing capabilities began in Python 3.5.

source_claims.title: Philosophy
source_claims.statement: The Zen of Python emphasizes explicitness, simplicity, readability and practical consistency, while remaining a guideline.

source_claims.title: PEPs
source_claims.statement: PEPs document information, processes, naming and language proposals and are overseen by the Steering Council.

source_claims.title: Syntax
source_claims.statement: Python uses significant indentation and provides statements for assignment, control flow, exceptions, classes, functions, context management, imports, matching and generators.

source_claims.title: Expressions and semantics
source_claims.statement: Python distinguishes expressions and statements and supports comprehensions, lambdas, slicing, unpacking, string forms and dynamic references.

source_claims.title: Typing
source_claims.statement: Python uses duck typing with typed objects and untyped names while remaining strongly typed; annotations may be checked externally.

source_claims.title: Built-in types
source_claims.statement: Python provides bool, bytearray, bytes, complex, dict, float, frozenset, int, list, NoneType, range, set, str and tuple.

source_claims.title: Numeric semantics
source_claims.statement: Python supports true/floor division, modulo, exponentiation, matrix multiplication, arbitrary precision integers, Decimal and Fraction.

source_claims.title: Libraries
source_claims.statement: The standard library covers Internet protocols/formats, GUI, relational databases, pseudorandom numbers, decimals, regex and unit testing.

source_claims.title: Environments
source_claims.statement: Python implementations commonly provide REPLs; CPython includes IDLE and the ecosystem includes IPython, Jupyter and desktop/web IDEs.

source_claims.title: CPython
source_claims.statement: CPython is the reference implementation, written in C, compiling Python to bytecode executed by a VM.

source_claims.title: Alternative implementations
source_claims.statement: The source describes PyPy, Codon, MicroPython, CircuitPython, Pyston, Cinder, RustPython and Stackless Python.

source_claims.title: Compilers and transpilers
source_claims.statement: The ecosystem includes Brython, Transcrypt, Cython, PyJL, Nuitka, Numba, Pythran, RPython and MyHDL.

source_claims.title: Performance
source_claims.statement: JIT, static compilation, multiprocessing, efficient data structures and native numerical libraries can improve performance.

source_claims.title: Development lifecycle
source_claims.statement: Python development uses PEPs, community review, GitHub and a release process with incompatible, feature and bug-fix releases.

source_claims.title: Culture and influence
source_claims.statement: PyCon, Monty Python naming/culture, Pythonic terminology and the influence graph are described.

source_claims.claim: PyTorch metadata identifies original authors, developer, release, stable version, languages, operating systems, architectures, license and official resources.
PyTorch is an open-source deep-learning library, successor to Torch, with high-level APIs over optimized low-level algorithms and CUDA bindings.
Tensor is fundamental; Autograd constructs a DAG during forward execution and backpropagates from loss.
PyTorch is popular alongside TensorFlow/Keras, installable with Anaconda, and named as the basis of several commercial systems.
Torch originated around 2001, evolved through Torch7/LuaTorch, and its refactoring was influenced by torch-autograd, HIPS/autograd and Chainer.
ONNX was created by Meta and Microsoft; Caffe2 later merged into PyTorch; independent foundation governance was announced in 2022.
PyTorch 2.0 introduced TorchDynamo as a Python-level compiler and reported performance improvements.
PyTorch tensors resemble NumPy arrays while supporting CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPUs and other GPU platforms such as AMD ROCm and Apple Metal.
torch.nn provides neural-network/training abstractions; networks inherit from nn.Module and define forward().
Serialization uses ZIP64 with model weights in Python pickle plus metadata such as byte order; .pt and .pth are used.
Source examples demonstrate CPU/cuda:0 devices and tensor creation, multiplication, sum, indexing and max.
Source neural-network example uses Flatten, Sequential, Linear, ReLU and returns logits.
